phy_ocra.11.0.summary: Every wave can be described using four quantities: **amplitude** (how big the disturbance is), **wavelength** (how long one complete wave is), **frequency** (how many waves pass a point each second) and **period** (how long one complete wave takes). Waves transfer **energy** from place to place without transferring matter, and these four quantities let you describe and compare any wave, from ripples on water to sound and light. You must be able to define each term precisely, read them from displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs, and use period = 1 / frequency.

core.p: A wave is a disturbance that transfers **energy** from one place to another. The particles (or fields) oscillate about a fixed position, but they do not travel along with the wave.
bullets: Waves transfer **energy and information**, not matter.
In a water wave, a floating cork bobs **up and down** but does not move along with the wave.
The **undisturbed position** (rest position) is where the medium would be with no wave.
Each point on the wave **oscillates** (vibrates) about its rest position.
Mechanical waves (sound, water, waves on a rope) need a medium; electromagnetic waves do not.
Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period apply to **all** waves.

callouts.p: Waves transfer energy from a source to a receiver; the medium itself does not travel with the wave.

core.p: Amplitude tells you how large the oscillation is. It is measured from the **middle (rest) position** to a crest or to a trough, never from crest to trough.
bullets: Amplitude is the **maximum displacement** of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position.
Measured in **metres** for water or rope waves (or other units of displacement).
For sound, a larger amplitude means a **louder** sound.
For light, a larger amplitude means a **brighter** light.
Larger amplitude means the wave carries **more energy**.
Amplitude does not affect wavelength, frequency or speed.

callouts.p: The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.

callouts.t: Crest to trough is NOT amplitude
callouts.p: The distance from crest to trough is **twice** the amplitude. Halve it to get the amplitude.

core.p: Wavelength is the length of one complete wave. You can measure it between any two matching points on neighbouring waves, as long as they are at the same stage of the oscillation.
bullets: Symbol: **lambda** (the Greek letter), measured in **metres (m)**.
Measured from **crest to crest**, **trough to trough**, or any point to the same point on the next wave.
For a longitudinal wave, measured from **one compression to the next** (or one rarefaction to the next).
On a displacement-distance graph, wavelength is read along the **distance** axis.
Shorter wavelength means more waves fit into the same distance.
Radio waves can have wavelengths of kilometres; gamma rays are smaller than an atom.

callouts.p: The distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, for example from one crest to the next crest.

core.p: Frequency tells you how often the oscillations happen. It is set by the **source** of the wave, and it does not change when the wave moves into a different medium.
bullets: Frequency is the **number of complete waves passing a point each second**.
Equivalently, the number of oscillations of the source per second.
Unit: **hertz (Hz)**; 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.
For sound, higher frequency means a **higher pitch**.
For visible light, frequency determines the **colour** (red has the lowest frequency, violet the highest).

callouts.p: The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).

core.p: The period is the time taken for **one complete wave** to pass a point (or for the source to make one complete oscillation). It is the opposite way of describing frequency: frequency counts waves per second, period gives seconds per wave.
bullets: Symbol: **T**, measured in **seconds (s)**.
**period = 1 / frequency**, so T = 1 / f.
Rearranged: **frequency = 1 / period**, so f = 1 / T.
High frequency means a **short** period; low frequency means a **long** period.
On a displacement-time graph, the period is read along the **time** axis between two crests.
Measure several periods and divide to reduce timing error (for example time 10 oscillations and divide by 10).

callouts.p: The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, measured in seconds (s).
period (s) = 1 / frequency (Hz), T = 1 / f

core.h: Crests, troughs and the rest position
core.p: Transverse waves are easiest to picture as a curve with high and low points. The labels on the curve are used in exam diagrams, so learn them exactly.
bullets: **Crest** (peak): the highest point of a transverse wave.
**Trough**: the lowest point of a transverse wave.
**Rest position** (undisturbed position): the central line the wave oscillates about.
Crest to next crest = one wavelength; crest to next trough = half a wavelength.
Vertical height from rest to crest = amplitude.
In a longitudinal wave, compressions and rarefactions play the same role as crests and troughs.

callouts.p: When a diagram shows several waves, count the number of **complete** waves before dividing the total length to find wavelength.

core.p: Both graphs look like the same wavy line, so the most important thing is to **read the x-axis label**. It tells you which quantity you can find from the repeat length.
bullets: **Displacement-distance** graph: a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant.
From it read **wavelength** (x-axis) and **amplitude** (y-axis).
**Displacement-time** graph: how one point on the wave moves over time.
From it read **period** (x-axis) and **amplitude** (y-axis).
Frequency is found from a displacement-time graph using f = 1 / T.
Wave speed needs both wavelength and frequency, so usually both types of information.

callouts.p: A common trap is quoting a 'wavelength' from a displacement-time graph. On a time axis the repeat length is the **period**.

core.p: Exam questions often show two waves and ask you to compare them. Look separately at the height (amplitude) and at how many waves fit in the same distance or time (wavelength or frequency).
bullets: Taller wave = **larger amplitude** = more energy, louder sound or brighter light.
More waves in the same **time** = higher frequency = shorter period.
More waves in the same **distance** = shorter wavelength.
For waves at the same speed, **higher frequency means shorter wavelength**.
Amplitude and frequency are **independent**: you can change one without changing the other.
On an oscilloscope trace of sound, height shows loudness and spacing shows pitch.

callouts.p: Making a wave bigger (amplitude) does not change how often it repeats (frequency).

fig.cap: Wave A has a larger amplitude; wave B has a smaller amplitude but twice the frequency, so twice as many waves fit in the same time.

core.p: This is a simple reciprocal relationship. Make sure units are in **seconds** and **hertz** before you calculate, converting milliseconds or kilohertz first.
bullets: Example: f = 50 Hz, so T = 1 / 50 = **0.02 s**.
Convert ms to s by dividing by 1000 (5 ms = 0.005 s).
Convert kHz to Hz by multiplying by 1000 (2 kHz = 2000 Hz).
Doubling the frequency **halves** the period.
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures, matching the data.

callouts.p: If the frequency is large, the period must be small. If your answer goes the other way, you have probably divided the wrong way round.

core.h: Measuring frequency and period in practice
core.p: For slow waves such as ripples, you can count waves passing a point with a stopwatch. For fast waves such as sound, an oscilloscope or data logger is used.
bullets: Count the number of waves passing a fixed mark in a measured time, then **frequency = number of waves / time**.
Time **many** oscillations and divide to find the period, which reduces the effect of reaction time.
A signal generator sets the frequency of a vibrating source directly.
An **oscilloscope** shows a displacement-time trace; use the time-base setting to convert squares to seconds.
Repeat and take a mean to reduce random error.
Use a fixed reference point so you count consistently.

callouts.p: Timing 10 waves instead of 1 makes the reaction-time error a much smaller fraction of the total time measured.

core.h: Linking the quantities to energy and perception
core.p: The quantities connect directly to what we hear and see, and examiners reward linking the physics term to the effect.
bullets: **Amplitude** links to the **energy** carried: larger amplitude, more energy.
Sound: amplitude gives **loudness**, frequency gives **pitch**.
Light: amplitude gives **brightness**, frequency gives **colour**.
Electromagnetic waves: higher frequency waves (such as X-rays) carry more energy per photon, which is why they are more hazardous.
Frequency is fixed by the source, so it is the quantity that stays the same when a wave changes medium.
Wavelength and speed can change when a wave enters a new medium.

analogy.t: A crowd doing a stadium wave
analogy.p: In a stadium wave each fan stands up and sits down in their own seat, yet the wave travels round the stadium. How high each fan jumps is the **amplitude**. The distance round the stadium from one standing group to the next is the **wavelength**. How many standing groups pass you each second is the **frequency**, and the time between you standing up one time and the next is the **period**. The fans stay in their seats, just as particles stay in place while energy travels. The analogy breaks down because real waves are smooth continuous oscillations, the fans choose when to move, and electromagnetic waves need no particles at all.

terms.d: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down motion about a fixed position.
The undisturbed position of the medium when no wave is present.
The distance and direction of a point on a wave from its rest position.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed position.
The distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave; symbol lambda, unit m.
The number of waves passing a point each second; unit hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point; symbol T, unit s.
The unit of frequency; one wave (oscillation) per second.
The highest point of a transverse wave.
The lowest point of a transverse wave.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are closer together.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are further apart.
A snapshot of a wave at one instant, showing displacement against position.
A graph showing how the displacement of one point on a wave changes over time.

mistakes.w: Amplitude is the distance from crest to trough.
mistakes.r: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position, which is half the crest-to-trough height.

mistakes.w: Wavelength is measured from a crest to the next trough.
mistakes.r: Crest to trough is half a wavelength; wavelength is crest to crest (same point to same point).

mistakes.w: Frequency is how fast the wave travels.
mistakes.r: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point per second; speed is a different quantity.

mistakes.w: Reading wavelength from a displacement-time graph.
mistakes.r: The repeat length on a time axis is the period, not the wavelength.

mistakes.w: T = f, or period = frequency x 1.
mistakes.r: Period = 1 / frequency.

mistakes.w: The water moves along with the wave.
mistakes.r: The water oscillates up and down about its rest position; only energy is transferred.

mistakes.w: A bigger amplitude means a higher frequency.
mistakes.r: Amplitude and frequency are independent; bigger amplitude means more energy (louder or brighter).

mistakes.w: Frequency is measured in seconds.
mistakes.r: Frequency is in hertz (Hz); period is in seconds.

exam.q: Define the amplitude of a wave.
model: Maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.
exam.tip: Include 'maximum' and 'from the rest position'.

exam.q: Define wavelength.
model: Distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave (for example crest to crest).
exam.tip: An example such as crest to crest is fine, but crest to trough loses the mark.

exam.q: State the unit of frequency.
model: Hertz (Hz).
exam.tip: Write the full name or the correct symbol with a capital H.

exam.q: Define the frequency of a wave.
model: The number of waves passing a point each second.
exam.tip: 'Per second' is essential.

exam.q: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz. Calculate its period.
exam.tip: Show the equation, then give the unit.

exam.q: The period of a sound wave is 2.5 ms. Calculate its frequency.
model: f = 400 Hz
exam.tip: Convert ms to s first; this is where most marks are lost.

exam.q: A diagram shows 4 complete waves across a distance of 2.0 m. The height from crest to trough is 0.30 m. Find the wavelength and the amplitude.
model: Wavelength = 2.0 / 4 = 0.5 m
Amplitude = 0.30 / 2 = 0.15 m
exam.tip: Halve crest-to-trough to get amplitude.

exam.q: Explain the difference between the information given by a displacement-distance graph and a displacement-time graph of the same wave.
model: Displacement-distance graph gives the wavelength (and amplitude).
Displacement-time graph gives the period (and amplitude), from which frequency can be found.
exam.tip: Name the quantity each x-axis repeat gives.

exam.q: Two sound waves are shown on an oscilloscope. Wave X has taller peaks; wave Y has peaks closer together. Compare what a listener would hear.
model: Wave X is louder because it has a larger amplitude.
Wave Y has a higher pitch because it has a higher frequency.
exam.tip: Link each physics quantity to a perception.

exam.q: Describe how a student could measure the frequency of water waves in a ripple tank and explain how to make the measurement more accurate.
model: Choose a fixed point / mark on the tank.
Count the number of waves passing that point in a measured time (for example 10 s) with a stopwatch.
Frequency = number of waves / time.
Count over a longer time or repeat and take a mean to reduce the effect of reaction time and random error.
exam.tip: Give the calculation step and one accuracy improvement.

exam.q: Explain, using the ideas of amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, how a wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Include how each quantity could be found from graphs.
model: Particles of the medium oscillate about their rest positions and pass energy on to neighbouring particles, so the particles do not travel with the wave.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position; larger amplitude means more energy is carried.
Wavelength is the distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, read from a displacement-distance graph.
Frequency is the number of waves passing a point per second, in Hz.
Period is the time for one complete wave to pass, read from a displacement-time graph.
Period and frequency are linked by T = 1 / f.
exam.tip: Structure your answer: energy transfer first, then each quantity with its definition and how to find it.

worked.q: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Calculate the period of the radio wave.
steps: Convert: 100 MHz = 100 000 000 Hz = 1.0 x 10^8 Hz
Use T = 1 / f

worked.q: An oscilloscope trace shows one complete wave across 4 squares. The time-base is set to 2 ms per square. Calculate the period and the frequency.
steps: Period = 4 squares x 2 ms = 8 ms
Convert: 8 ms = 0.008 s
f = 125 Hz

worked.q: A student times 20 waves passing a buoy in 50 s. Find the frequency and the period, and explain why timing 20 waves is better than timing 1.
steps: Frequency = number of waves / time = 20 / 50 = 0.4 Hz
Reaction time error is about the same whether timing 1 wave or 20.
Over a longer total time, the error is a smaller fraction, so the result is more accurate.
worked.ans: f = 0.4 Hz, T = 2.5 s; timing 20 waves reduces the percentage effect of reaction time.

phy_ocra.11.1.summary: The **wave speed equation** links how fast a wave travels to its frequency and wavelength: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) x wavelength (m)**, or v = f x lambda. It works for every type of wave, from ripples and sound to light, and must be recalled and rearranged without a formula sheet. In PAG P4 you measure wave speeds in the lab, for example ripples in a ripple tank, waves on a stretched string and the speed of sound in air, using either v = f x lambda or speed = distance / time.

core.p: Each second, a source sends out f complete waves, and each one is lambda metres long. So in one second the front of the wave moves f x lambda metres, which is the wave speed.
bullets: **wave speed = frequency x wavelength**
Symbols: **v = f x lambda**
v in **metres per second (m/s)**, f in **hertz (Hz)**, lambda in **metres (m)**.
This equation must be **recalled**: it is not given on the equation sheet.
It applies to **all waves**: transverse and longitudinal, mechanical and electromagnetic.
Wave speed is the speed at which **energy** is transferred (the speed the wave moves through the medium).

callouts.p: wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) x wavelength (m)
The distance travelled by a wave (its energy) per unit time.

fig.cap: Formula triangle for v = f x lambda. Cover the quantity you want: v = f x lambda, f = v / lambda, lambda = v / f.

core.p: You will often be given two of the three quantities and asked to find the third. Rearrange before substituting.
bullets: **v = f x lambda** to find speed.
**f = v / lambda** to find frequency.
**lambda = v / f** to find wavelength.
For a fixed speed, f and lambda are **inversely proportional**: double the frequency and the wavelength halves.
Always write the equation first, then substitute, then give the answer with a unit.
Higher tier questions may combine this with T = 1 / f or speed = distance / time.

callouts.p: Even if the final answer is wrong, writing the equation and correct substitution usually earns marks.

core.p: Most lost marks come from forgetting to convert. Put every quantity into **Hz, m and m/s** before you calculate.
bullets: **kHz to Hz**: multiply by 1000 (3.4 kHz = 3400 Hz).
**MHz to Hz**: multiply by 1 000 000 (90 MHz = 9.0 x 10^7 Hz).
**GHz to Hz**: multiply by 10^9.
**cm to m**: divide by 100 (2.5 cm = 0.025 m).
**mm to m**: divide by 1000; **nm to m**: multiply by 10^-9.
Give answers in **standard form** when numbers are very large or very small.

callouts.p: Substituting 2.5 cm as 2.5 instead of 0.025 m gives an answer 100 times too big.

core.p: Wave speed can also be found directly by timing how long a wave takes to travel a measured distance. This is the method used for the speed of sound and for timing ripples across a tank.
bullets: **wave speed = distance / time**, v = d / t.
For an **echo**, the sound travels to the reflector and back, so distance = **2 x** the distance to the wall.
Use a long distance so the time is large compared with reaction time.
Both methods give the same speed for the same wave in the same medium.
Combining both: if you know v from timing and f from the source, you can calculate lambda.
A wave front travels at the wave speed; individual particles do not.

callouts.p: In echo questions double the distance to the wall, because the sound goes there and back.

core.p: Knowing typical speeds helps you check whether an answer is sensible.
bullets: All **electromagnetic waves** travel at **3.0 x 10^8 m/s** in a vacuum (and almost this in air).
**Sound in air**: about **330 to 340 m/s** at room temperature.
Sound travels **faster in liquids and solids** than in gases.
**Ripples** on water in a ripple tank: typically a few **cm/s to tens of cm/s**.
Waves on a stretched string: depends on tension; typically **tens of m/s**.
If you calculate the speed of sound as 3 m/s or 3000 m/s in air, check your units.

callouts.p: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, so higher frequency EM waves must have shorter wavelengths.

core.p: The speed of a wave depends on the **medium** it travels through, not on the source. The source sets the **frequency**.
bullets: Changing the source frequency in the same medium changes the **wavelength**, not the speed.
Moving into a new medium changes the **speed** and **wavelength**; frequency stays the same.
Water waves travel **slower in shallow water** than in deep water.
Sound travels faster in warmer air.
Light slows down when it enters glass or water.
This change of speed at a boundary is what causes **refraction**.

callouts.t: Frequency is set by the source
callouts.p: When a wave crosses into a new medium its frequency does not change; v and lambda change in proportion.

core.p: A ripple tank makes waves visible. A lamp above the tank projects bright and dark bands (crests and troughs) onto paper below so they can be measured.
bullets: A motor with a **dipper** (or straight bar) vibrates on the surface to make ripples; the frequency is set by the power supply or signal generator.
A **lamp** above the tank casts a shadow pattern on a sheet of paper below.
Measure the length of **several (for example 10) wavelengths** with a ruler on the pattern, then divide to find one wavelength.
Find frequency by counting waves passing a point in 10 s, or read it from the signal generator.
Calculate **v = f x lambda**.
A **stroboscope** (or a photograph or video) can freeze the pattern to make measuring easier.

callouts.p: Measuring across 10 waves and dividing by 10 reduces the uncertainty in the wavelength compared with measuring one.
Water and mains electricity: keep the power supply away from spills and mop up water to prevent slips.

core.h: PAG P4: speed of sound in air
core.p: Sound travels too fast to time over a short distance with a stopwatch, so you need either a large distance (echo method) or electronic timing (two microphones).
bullets: **Echo method**: stand at least 50 m from a large flat wall, clap and time the echo; or clap in rhythm with the echoes and time 20 claps.
Speed = **2 x distance to wall / time** for one echo.
**Two-microphone method**: place two microphones a measured distance apart connected to an oscilloscope or fast timer; the time delay between signals gives v = d / t.
**Oscilloscope method**: a signal generator drives a loudspeaker; move one microphone until the traces line up again, the distance moved is one wavelength; then v = f x lambda.
Measure distances with a trundle wheel or tape measure.
Repeat and take a mean to reduce random error; human reaction time is the main source of error in manual timing.

callouts.p: Timing many echoes (for example 20 claps) rather than one reduces the effect of reaction time on the result.

core.h: PAG P4: waves on a stretched string
core.p: A vibration generator driven by a signal generator shakes one end of a string that passes over a pulley with masses hanging from it. At certain frequencies a steady (stationary) wave pattern of loops appears.
bullets: Adjust the frequency until a clear pattern of loops forms.
Each loop is **half a wavelength**, so one wavelength = the length of **two loops**.
Measure the length of several loops with a metre rule and calculate lambda.
Read the frequency from the **signal generator**.
Calculate **v = f x lambda**.
Keep the hanging mass (tension) and length of string the same, because they affect the wave speed.

core.h: Errors and improvements in wave speed practicals
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to evaluate a method. Identify the biggest source of uncertainty and suggest a specific improvement.
bullets: **Reaction time** in manual timing: time over a longer distance or many cycles, or use electronic timing.
Measuring a single wavelength: measure **across many wavelengths** and divide.
Moving ripple pattern: use a **stroboscope** or photograph next to a ruler.
Echo confused with other reflections: use a large, flat wall in an open space.
Wind affects sound speed outdoors: repeat in both directions or on a still day.
Repeat readings, discard anomalies and calculate a **mean**.

callouts.p: 'Use a stroboscope to freeze the waves' scores; 'be more accurate' does not.

core.h: Proportional reasoning with v = f x lambda
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain what happens to one quantity when another changes, without needing a full calculation.
bullets: Same medium, frequency doubled: speed unchanged, so wavelength **halves**.
Same medium, frequency tripled: wavelength becomes **one third**.
Wave enters a slower medium: frequency unchanged, so wavelength **decreases** in proportion to speed.
EM spectrum: all same speed, so gamma rays (highest f) have the **shortest** wavelength.
Graph of lambda against 1 / f for one medium is a straight line through the origin with gradient v.
Graph of v against f in one medium is a horizontal line, because speed does not depend on frequency.

callouts.p: In one medium v is constant, so f x lambda is constant: if one goes up, the other goes down by the same factor.

analogy.t: People walking on a conveyor of footsteps
analogy.p: Think of a person walking: their speed equals how many steps they take per second (frequency) times the length of each step (wavelength). Take more steps per second with the same stride and you go faster. For a wave, though, the medium fixes the speed, so if the source makes the steps quicker, each step has to get shorter to keep the same speed. The analogy breaks down because a walker carries their own body along, whereas a wave carries only energy, and a walker can choose their speed while a wave's speed is set by the medium.

mistakes.w: v = f / lambda or v = lambda / f.
mistakes.r: v = f x lambda.

mistakes.w: Using a wavelength in cm without converting to m.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres before substituting into v = f x lambda.

mistakes.w: Using kHz directly in the equation.
mistakes.r: Convert kHz to Hz (multiply by 1000) first.

mistakes.w: Increasing the frequency increases the speed of the wave.
mistakes.r: In the same medium the speed stays the same; the wavelength decreases.

mistakes.w: For an echo, using the distance to the wall once.
mistakes.r: Sound travels there and back, so distance = 2 x distance to the wall.

mistakes.r: One loop is half a wavelength; one wavelength is two loops.

mistakes.w: Measuring one wavelength in the ripple tank to get an accurate value.

mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda).
exam.tip: Words or correct symbols both score.

exam.q: A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate its speed.
model: v = 2 m/s
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 850 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
model: lambda = v / f
lambda = 340 / 850
lambda = 0.4 m
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: A radio wave has a wavelength of 1500 m. Radio waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate the frequency in kHz.
model: f = 200 kHz
exam.tip: Watch the requested unit.

exam.q: Ripples in a tank have a wavelength of 2.0 cm and frequency 12 Hz. Calculate their speed in m/s.
exam.tip: Convert cm to m first.

exam.q: The frequency of a wave in a ripple tank is doubled. State and explain what happens to the wavelength.
model: The wavelength halves.
Speed depends on the medium so stays the same; v = f x lambda so if f doubles lambda halves.
exam.tip: State the speed is constant to justify the answer.

exam.q: A student stands 85 m from a wall. The echo of a clap returns after 0.50 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
model: Total distance = 2 x 85 = 170 m
exam.tip: Doubling the distance is the key step.

exam.q: Describe how a ripple tank can be used to measure the speed of water waves.
model: Set the dipper vibrating at a known frequency (from the signal generator / count waves passing a point in 10 s).
Use a lamp to project the wave pattern onto paper below.
Measure the length of 10 wavelengths with a ruler and divide by 10.
Calculate speed using v = f x lambda.
exam.tip: Give how f and lambda are each found, then the equation.

exam.q: Suggest why the echo method uses a distance of at least 50 m from the wall.
model: So the time is long enough to measure.
Reaction time is then a small fraction of the time measured, so the result is more accurate.
exam.tip: Link distance to time and to reaction time.

exam.q: On a stretched string experiment, 4 loops cover 1.2 m when the frequency is 60 Hz. Calculate the wave speed.
model: Each loop = 1.2 / 4 = 0.3 m = half a wavelength
lambda = 0.6 m
exam.tip: Remember one loop is half a wavelength.

exam.q: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air in a school laboratory or playground. Include how to reduce errors and how to calculate the speed.
model: Stand a measured distance (at least 50 m, measured with a trundle wheel) from a large flat wall.
Clap and time the echo, or clap in time with echoes and time 20 claps.
Total distance travelled per echo = 2 x distance to wall.
Speed = total distance / time.
Reduce reaction time error by timing many claps and repeating to find a mean.
Alternatively, use two microphones a measured distance apart with an oscilloscope or fast timer to measure the time delay and calculate v = d / t.
exam.tip: For 6 marks give a clear sequence, the calculation, and at least one improvement.

worked.q: Green light has a wavelength of 530 nm. Calculate its frequency. Speed of light = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
steps: f = v / lambda

worked.q: In a ripple tank, a student measures 8 wavelengths across 12 cm. The dipper vibrates at 5.0 Hz. Calculate the wave speed.
steps: One wavelength = 12 / 8 = 1.5 cm
Convert: 1.5 cm = 0.015 m
v = f x lambda = 5.0 x 0.015

worked.q: A sound of frequency 680 Hz travels from air (340 m/s) into water (1500 m/s). Calculate the wavelength in each medium and explain the difference.
steps: Frequency stays 680 Hz in both media.
In air: lambda = 340 / 680 = 0.50 m
In water: lambda = 1500 / 680 = 2.2 m (2 s.f.)
Sound travels faster in water, and f is fixed, so the wavelength is longer.
worked.ans: 0.50 m in air and 2.2 m in water; the wavelength increases because the speed increases while frequency stays the same.

phy_ocra.11.2.summary: Waves come in two types, defined by the direction of the oscillations compared with the direction the wave transfers energy. In a **transverse** wave the oscillations are **perpendicular** (at 90 degrees) to the direction of energy transfer, as in ripples on water, waves on a string and all electromagnetic waves. In a **longitudinal** wave the oscillations are **parallel** to the direction of energy transfer, producing **compressions** and **rarefactions**, as in sound waves. In both types energy is transferred but the medium itself is not carried along.

core.p: Both transverse and longitudinal waves transfer **energy** from a source to somewhere else. The particles of the medium **oscillate about fixed positions** and pass the energy on to their neighbours, but they do not travel with the wave.
bullets: A cork on a pond bobs **up and down** as ripples pass, but stays in roughly the same place.
Air particles in a sound wave vibrate **back and forth** but do not travel from the speaker to your ear.
The wave is the **pattern** of disturbance moving through the medium.
Electromagnetic waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields, so they need **no medium**.
The difference between the two types is only the **direction** of the oscillations.
Both types can be described with amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed.

callouts.p: To classify a wave, compare the **direction of oscillation** with the **direction of energy transfer** (the direction the wave travels).

core.p: In a transverse wave the particles (or fields) move **at right angles** to the direction the energy travels. Shake a rope or slinky side to side and a transverse wave runs along it.
bullets: Oscillations are **perpendicular** to the direction of energy transfer.
Have **crests** (peaks) and **troughs**.
Examples: **ripples on water**, waves on a **string or rope**, **all electromagnetic waves** (light, radio, X-rays and so on).
Seismic **S-waves** are transverse.
Electromagnetic transverse waves can travel through a **vacuum**.
Mechanical transverse waves need a medium; S-waves cannot travel through liquids.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

core.p: In a longitudinal wave the particles move **back and forth along the same line** as the energy travels. Push and pull one end of a slinky and pulses of squashed-up coils travel along it.
bullets: Oscillations are **parallel** to the direction of energy transfer.
Have **compressions** (particles close together, higher pressure) and **rarefactions** (particles spread out, lower pressure).
Examples: **sound waves**, **ultrasound**, seismic **P-waves**, pushing and pulling a slinky.
Always need a **medium** (solid, liquid or gas); they cannot travel through a vacuum.
Wavelength is the distance from **one compression to the next** compression (or rarefaction to rarefaction).
P-waves can travel through solids and liquids.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A compression is a region where particles are closer together; a rarefaction is a region where particles are further apart.

fig.cap: A longitudinal wave on a slinky. The coils move back and forth parallel to the direction of energy transfer, making compressions and rarefactions. One wavelength is from one compression to the next.

core.p: Most exam questions on this point ask you to state a difference or classify a wave. Learn the comparison table.
bullets: The **only defining difference** is the direction of oscillation relative to energy transfer.
Transverse: up and down (or side to side) while the wave moves forwards.
Longitudinal: backwards and forwards along the direction the wave moves.
Both transfer energy without transferring matter.
Both obey v = f x lambda.
Both can be reflected and refracted.

callouts.p: Mark schemes want **perpendicular** (or at right angles) for transverse and **parallel** (or in the same direction) for longitudinal, both compared with the **direction of energy transfer**.

core.p: A loudspeaker cone vibrates backwards and forwards. Moving forward it pushes air particles together (a compression); moving back it leaves a region where they are spread out (a rarefaction). These pressure variations travel through the air.
bullets: Sound is produced by **vibrating** objects.
Air particles oscillate **parallel** to the direction the sound travels.
Compressions are regions of **higher pressure**; rarefactions are regions of **lower pressure**.
Sound needs a medium, so it **cannot travel through a vacuum** (a ringing bell in a jar goes quiet as air is pumped out).
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
The frequency of the vibrating source gives the frequency (pitch) of the sound.

callouts.p: Oscilloscope traces of sound look like transverse waves, but that is a graph of pressure or voltage against time. The sound wave itself is longitudinal.

core.h: Demonstrating both types with a slinky
core.p: A slinky spring is the standard way to show both wave types in the lab, and exam questions often describe it.
bullets: Lay the slinky on a smooth floor or bench with a partner holding the far end.
**Transverse**: move your hand **side to side**, perpendicular to the slinky; a wave travels along it.
**Longitudinal**: move your hand **forwards and backwards** along the line of the slinky; compressions and rarefactions travel along it.
Tie a ribbon or mark on one coil: it oscillates about a fixed position but does not travel along the slinky.
The ribbon moves perpendicular to the slinky for a transverse wave and parallel to it for a longitudinal wave.
This is **evidence that the wave transfers energy, not the material**.

callouts.p: In a 'describe how' question, state how the hand moves relative to the slinky and what the marked coil does.

core.p: All electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma rays, are transverse. The oscillating quantities are electric and magnetic fields at right angles to the direction of travel.
bullets: EM waves do **not need a medium** and can travel through a vacuum.
All EM waves travel at the **same speed** in a vacuum: 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
Light from the Sun reaches Earth through the vacuum of space; sound could not.
Because they are transverse, light waves can be **polarised** (a property only transverse waves have).
Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all transverse.
Do not confuse EM waves with sound: sound is longitudinal and needs a medium.

callouts.p: Light is a transverse EM wave and can travel through a vacuum; sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave and cannot.

core.p: Earthquakes produce both types of wave, which makes them a useful example of the difference.
bullets: **P-waves** (primary) are **longitudinal** and travel through solids and liquids.
**S-waves** (secondary) are **transverse** and travel through solids only.
P-waves are faster than S-waves, so they arrive at detectors first.
S-waves not passing through the outer core is evidence that the outer core is liquid.
Transverse mechanical waves need a rigid medium, which is why S-waves are stopped by liquids.
This shows that the type of wave affects which materials it can travel through.

callouts.p: P-waves Push and pull (longitudinal); S-waves Shake side to Side (transverse).

core.p: Ripples on the surface of water are treated as **transverse** at GCSE. The water surface moves up and down as the ripple travels outwards.
bullets: A floating object moves **up and down** as a ripple passes, showing the oscillation is perpendicular to the energy transfer.
The object is **not carried along**, showing the water does not travel with the wave.
Ripple tanks use water waves to show reflection and refraction.
Crests show as bright lines in a ripple tank because they focus the light like lenses.
Wavelength is measured from crest to crest.
Water waves slow down in shallower water.

callouts.t: Evidence that waves transfer energy, not matter
callouts.p: A floating object bobs up and down in the same place as water waves pass, so the water itself is not moving along with the wave.

core.p: When given an unfamiliar wave, ask: in which direction do the particles move compared with the direction the energy goes?
bullets: Particle motion **at 90 degrees** to energy transfer: **transverse**.
Particle motion **along the same line** as energy transfer: **longitudinal**.
If the question shows compressions and rarefactions, it is longitudinal.
If the question shows crests and troughs of a physical displacement, it is transverse.
Mention the **direction of energy transfer** (or the direction of wave travel) in every definition.
Graphs of displacement against distance can represent either type, so read the context.

callouts.p: 'Transverse waves go up and down' gains no marks. You must compare the oscillation with the direction of energy transfer.

analogy.t: A queue and a Mexican wave
analogy.p: A **Mexican wave** in a stadium is like a transverse wave: each fan stands up and sits down (vertical) while the wave moves round the stadium (horizontal). A **queue being jostled** is like a longitudinal wave: someone at the back gives a push, each person bumps forward into the next and then steps back, so a squash of people (a compression) travels along the queue, followed by a gap (a rarefaction). In both cases people stay in roughly the same place but the disturbance moves. The analogy breaks down because people react with a delay and choose to move, whereas particles pass on energy through forces, and EM waves need no particles at all.

exam.q: State what is meant by a transverse wave.
model: Oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
exam.tip: Must compare with the direction of energy transfer.

exam.q: State what is meant by a longitudinal wave.
model: Oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
exam.tip: 'Parallel' is the key word.

exam.q: Give one example of a transverse wave and one example of a longitudinal wave.
model: Transverse: light / any EM wave / water ripples / waves on a string / S-wave.
Longitudinal: sound / ultrasound / P-wave.
exam.tip: Avoid vague examples like 'a wave in the sea'.

exam.q: Name the regions of a longitudinal wave where particles are close together and where they are far apart.
model: Close together: compression.
Far apart: rarefaction.
exam.tip: Spell rarefaction carefully.

exam.q: Describe how a slinky spring can be used to show a longitudinal wave.
model: Move one end backwards and forwards along the length of the slinky.
Compressions and rarefactions travel along the slinky.
exam.tip: State the direction of the hand movement.

exam.q: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum but light can.
model: Sound is a mechanical (longitudinal) wave that needs particles to vibrate.
A vacuum has no particles.
Light is an electromagnetic wave which does not need a medium.
exam.tip: Contrast the two types of wave.

exam.q: A student places a small cork on water in a ripple tank. Describe the motion of the cork as waves pass and explain what this shows.
model: The cork moves up and down.
It stays in the same place / is not carried along.
This shows the wave transfers energy but not the water (matter); and the wave is transverse.
exam.tip: Link the observation to energy transfer.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave, using a diagram description for each.
model: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
Transverse has crests and troughs, e.g. a wave on a rope.
Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
Longitudinal has compressions and rarefactions, e.g. sound.
exam.tip: Give the definition and a feature for each type.

exam.q: S-waves from an earthquake do not reach the opposite side of the Earth. Suggest why.
model: S-waves are transverse.
Transverse (mechanical) waves cannot travel through liquids, and the outer core is liquid.
exam.tip: Link wave type to the medium.

exam.q: A loudspeaker produces a sound wave. Describe how the air particles move and how compressions and rarefactions are formed.
model: The cone vibrates backwards and forwards.
When it moves forward it pushes air particles together, forming a compression.
When it moves back particles spread out, forming a rarefaction; particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
exam.tip: Mention parallel oscillation for full marks.

exam.q: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves. Your answer should include how the particles move, the features of each wave, examples and whether a medium is needed.
model: Both transfer energy without transferring matter; particles oscillate about fixed positions.
Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, with crests and troughs.
Examples of transverse: EM waves, water ripples, waves on a string, S-waves.
Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions.
Examples of longitudinal: sound, ultrasound, P-waves.
EM transverse waves can travel through a vacuum; longitudinal waves such as sound always need a medium.
exam.tip: Use a structured comparison: similarities, then each type with direction, features, examples, medium.

worked.q: Classify each wave as transverse or longitudinal: (a) microwaves, (b) ultrasound, (c) a wave on a guitar string, (d) a P-wave.
steps: (a) Microwaves are electromagnetic, and all EM waves are transverse.
(b) Ultrasound is sound above 20 kHz; sound is longitudinal.
(c) The string moves at right angles to the direction the wave travels: transverse.
(d) P-waves push and pull the rock along the direction of travel: longitudinal.

worked.q: A diagram of a slinky shows compressions at 10 cm, 40 cm and 70 cm from one end. The hand at one end makes 2 oscillations per second. Find the wavelength and the wave speed.
steps: Wavelength = distance between neighbouring compressions = 40 - 10 = 30 cm
Convert: 30 cm = 0.30 m
Frequency = 2 Hz
v = f x lambda = 2 x 0.30 = 0.60 m/s

worked.q: Model answer: describe an experiment using a slinky and a ribbon to show the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, and to show that waves do not transfer matter.
steps: Stretch a slinky along a bench with a partner holding the far end, and tie a ribbon to one coil in the middle.
Move one end side to side: a transverse wave travels along and the ribbon moves side to side, at right angles to the slinky.
Move one end backwards and forwards: a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions travels along and the ribbon moves back and forth, parallel to the slinky.
In both cases the ribbon returns to its starting position and does not move along the slinky.
worked.ans: The ribbon shows the direction of oscillation (perpendicular for transverse, parallel for longitudinal) and, because it is not carried along, that waves transfer energy but not matter.

phy_ocra.11.3.summary: When sound waves travel from one medium into another, such as from air into water or a solid wall, their speed and wavelength change while their frequency remains constant. This change in speed causes the waves to change direction, a phenomenon known as refraction, and results in partial reflection and transmission at the boundary. Understanding these boundary behaviors is essential for explaining how sonar operates, why sound behaves differently in various materials, and how seismic waves travel through the Earth.

core.p: Sound waves are longitudinal waves that require a medium to travel through. When a sound wave meets a boundary between two different media, part of the wave is reflected, and part is transmitted into the second medium, where its speed and wavelength change.
bullets: Sound requires particles to oscillate; thus, it cannot travel through a vacuum.
Different media have different densities and elastic properties, affecting how fast sound travels.
At any boundary, energy is shared between the reflected wave and the transmitted wave.

callouts.p: The total energy of the incident wave equals the sum of the energies of the reflected and transmitted waves.

core.h: 2. What Happens to Frequency at a Boundary?
core.p: When a sound wave crosses a boundary into a new medium, its frequency remains completely unchanged. Frequency is determined entirely by the source producing the sound and cannot be altered by the medium it travels through.
bullets: Source determines frequency: If a tuning fork vibrates at 440 Hz, the sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz in air, water, and steel.
Vibration rate matches: The particles at the boundary are forced to vibrate at the exact same frequency as the incoming wave.
Constant frequency is the foundational rule for wave boundary calculations.

callouts.p: Never state that frequency changes when a wave crosses a boundary; only speed and wavelength change.

core.h: 3. Changes in Wave Speed Across Media
core.p: The speed of sound depends strongly on the medium's density and stiffness. In general, sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases because particles are closer together in denser, stiffer materials.
bullets: Speed in air is approximately 340 m/s at room temperature.
Speed in water is about 1500 m/s because water molecules are more tightly bound than gas molecules.
Speed in steel is around 5000 m/s due to very strong elastic forces between iron atoms.

callouts.p: Wave speed is the distance travelled by a wave per second, calculated as v = f times lambda.

core.h: 4. The Wave Equation and Wavelength Scaling
core.p: Because the wave speed (v) changes across a boundary while frequency (f) stays constant, the wavelength (lambda) must change proportionally according to the wave equation v = f * lambda.
bullets: If speed increases upon entering a new medium, wavelength must also increase.
If speed decreases, wavelength must decrease by the exact same factor.
Wavelength is directly proportional to wave speed since frequency is constant.

callouts.p: Since v = f * lambda and f is constant, v is directly proportional to lambda.

core.p: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary at an angle, caused by the change in wave speed as it enters a different medium.
bullets: When sound passes from a slower medium into a faster medium, it bends away from the normal.
When sound passes from a faster medium into a slower medium, it bends towards the normal.
Refraction explains why sounds can sometimes be heard over much greater distances at night.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another at an angle, due to a change in speed.

core.p: Acoustic impedance (Z) is a measure of how much resistance a medium offers to the flow of sound waves, calculated as the product of density and wave speed (Z = rho * v).
bullets: A large difference in acoustic impedance between two media results in strong reflection and weak transmission.
A small difference in impedance results in most of the sound being transmitted and little reflected.
Air and human tissue have very different acoustic impedances, requiring gel during ultrasound scans.

callouts.p: Acoustic impedance Z = rho * v, where rho is density and v is wave speed.

core.p: When sound hits a hard boundary, it reflects according to the law of reflection, where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. This is the underlying principle behind echoes and echolocation.
bullets: Hard surfaces like concrete walls or cave walls are excellent reflectors of sound.
Soft materials like foam or carpets absorb sound and reduce reflections.
Echo sounding uses reflected sound pulses to measure water depth or locate objects.

callouts.p: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, measured relative to the normal.

core.p: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves above 20,000 Hz. When these waves cross boundaries between different tissues in the body, partial reflections occur, which are detected to build real-time images.
bullets: A coupling gel is applied to the skin to match acoustic impedance and prevent reflection at the air-skin boundary.
Different internal tissues (muscle, bone, blood, fat) have different densities, creating clear boundary reflections.
Safe non-ionizing technique used for prenatal scans and diagnostic imaging.

callouts.p: Always explain the role of acoustic matching gel when discussing medical ultrasound scans.

core.p: SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) relies on transmitting sound pulses through water and timing how long the reflected echo takes to return from the seabed or submerged objects.
bullets: Distance is calculated using the equation distance = speed * time / 2 (dividing by 2 because the sound travels to the target and back).
Used by ships to map the ocean floor and detect submarines.
Low frequency sonar travels vast distances underwater.

callouts.p: d = (v * t) / 2 is essential for calculating depths using echo times.

core.p: Earthquakes produce seismic waves (P-waves and S-waves) that travel through the Earth. As they cross boundaries between different mantle and core layers, they refract and reflect, providing evidence for the Earth's internal structure.
bullets: P-waves are longitudinal and can travel through both solids and liquids.
S-waves are transverse and can only travel through solids, stopping at the liquid outer core boundary.
Abrupt changes in wave speeds reveal the boundaries between crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.

callouts.p: Shadow zones for S-waves prove that the Earth's outer core is liquid.

core.p: When sound interacts with a boundary, transmission allows the wave to continue into the new medium, while absorption converts some acoustic energy into thermal energy within the material.
bullets: Transmission efficiency depends on the matching of acoustic impedances.
Absorption turns organized particle oscillations into random thermal motion.
Soundproofing materials combine absorption and reflection properties to block noise.

callouts.p: The process where wave energy is taken up by a material and converted into thermal energy.

analogy.t: Marching band crossing a muddy field
analogy.p: Imagine a marching band walking in straight rows from a smooth pavement (fast medium) onto a muddy field (slow medium) at an angle. The musicians on one side hit the mud first and slow down, while the others on the pavement are still moving fast. This speed difference causes the entire line of musicians to pivot and change direction (refraction). Furthermore, their stride length (wavelength) gets shorter in the mud, but the number of steps taken per minute (frequency) stays exactly the same. However, this analogy breaks down because sound wave particles only oscillate back and forth about a fixed point rather than walking forward through the medium.

terms.d: The product of the density of a medium and the speed of sound within that medium.
An interface separating two different media with different physical properties.
A reflection of sound waves off a hard surface, heard after the direct sound.
The number of complete wave oscillations passing a point per second, measured in Hertz.
An imaginary line perpendicular to a boundary at the point where a wave strikes it.
The change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary at an angle due to a change in speed.
A technique using sound propagation to navigate, communicate, or detect objects underwater.
The passing of wave energy through a medium or across a boundary into a new medium.
Sound waves with frequencies higher than the upper limit of human hearing, above 20,000 Hz.
The speed at which wave energy travels through a medium, measured in metres per second.
The distance between two corresponding points on consecutive waves, measured in metres.
Shock waves generated by earthquakes that travel through the Earth's interior and crust.

mistakes.w: Saying frequency changes when sound crosses a boundary.
mistakes.r: Frequency is determined entirely by the source and remains constant across all media.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to divide by 2 in sonar calculations.
mistakes.r: Remember that the sonar pulse travels to the target and back, so the total time must be halved for distance to one-way depth.

mistakes.w: Stating that sound travels faster in gases than in solids.
mistakes.r: Sound travels fastest in solids because particles are closer together and bonds are stronger.

mistakes.w: Confusing transverse and longitudinal sound waves.
mistakes.r: Sound waves are strictly longitudinal; particles oscillate parallel to energy propagation.

mistakes.w: Saying reflection only happens with light.
mistakes.r: Sound waves also reflect off boundaries, producing echoes.

mistakes.w: Stating wavelength stays the same during refraction.
mistakes.r: Because speed changes while frequency is constant, wavelength must change proportionally (v = f * lambda).

mistakes.w: Believing ultrasound can travel through a vacuum.
mistakes.r: Ultrasound is a sound wave and therefore requires a physical medium of particles to travel.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the frequency and wavelength of a sound wave when it passes from air into water.
model: Frequency remains constant
Because frequency is determined by the source
Wave speed increases in water
Therefore wavelength increases because v = f * lambda
exam.tip: Always link the change in wavelength directly to the constant frequency and increasing speed using the wave equation.

exam.q: A sound wave travels from air into a concrete wall. Describe the changes to the wave.
model: Part of the wave is reflected and part is transmitted
Speed of sound increases significantly in concrete
Wavelength increases while frequency remains unchanged
exam.tip: Mention both reflection and transmission alongside the changes in speed and wavelength.

exam.q: Calculate the depth of the ocean if a sonar pulse takes 0.4 seconds to return to a ship. The speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s.
model: Distance = speed * time
Total distance = 1500 * 0.4 = 600 m
exam.tip: Show your division by 2 clearly to secure the final method mark.

exam.q: Explain why ultrasound gel is applied to a patient's skin before a scan.
model: Air and skin have very different acoustic impedances
Without gel, most ultrasound would be reflected at the skin-air boundary
Gel matches acoustic impedance so more ultrasound enters the body
exam.tip: Use the term acoustic impedance to gain full credit in OCR exams.

exam.q: Define acoustic impedance and state its unit.
model: Product of density and speed of sound
Unit is kg/(m^2 s) or Rayls
exam.tip: Learn the formula Z = rho * v to help recall the definition.

exam.q: Describe how seismic P-waves provide evidence for the Earth's structure when crossing boundaries.
model: P-waves are longitudinal waves
They change speed abruptly at boundaries between mantle and core layers
This causes refraction of the wave paths
Proves that the Earth has different layers with varying densities and states
exam.tip: Mention refraction and speed changes caused by density variations.

exam.q: State the law of reflection for sound waves.
model: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
Angles are measured relative to the normal
exam.tip: Always specify that angles are measured from the normal line.

exam.q: Explain why sound travels faster in steel than in air.
model: Steel has much stronger elastic bonds between particles
Particles are much closer together, allowing vibrations to pass faster
exam.tip: Reference both particle proximity and elastic stiffness.

exam.q: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m in air. Calculate its speed.
model: v = f * lambda
exam.tip: State the formula, substitute numbers, and include correct units.

worked.q: A sound wave with a frequency of 200 Hz passes from air (speed 340 m/s) into water (speed 1500 m/s). Calculate its wavelength in air and in water.
steps: Step 1: Use v = f * lambda to find wavelength in air. lambda = v / f = 340 / 200 = 1.7 m.
Step 2: Note that frequency remains constant at 200 Hz in water.
Step 3: Use v = f * lambda to find wavelength in water. lambda = v / f = 1500 / 200 = 7.5 m.
worked.ans: Wavelength in air is 1.7 m and in water is 7.5 m.

worked.q: A research vessel sends a pulse of ultrasound into the ocean. The echo returns after 0.80 seconds. If the average speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s, calculate the depth of the seabed.
steps: Step 1: Calculate total distance travelled by the pulse using distance = speed * time.
Step 2: Distance = 1500 m/s * 0.80 s = 1200 metres.
Step 3: Divide by 2 because the wave travelled down to the seabed and back up to the ship.
Step 4: Depth = 1200 / 2 = 600 metres.
worked.ans: The depth of the seabed is 600 metres.

phy_ocra.11.5.summary: This topic covers how sound travels through solids via particle vibrations, the mechanism of human hearing across our finite frequency range, and the physics of ultrasound and infrasound. Students must master how density and elasticity affect wave speed in solid media and why human ears lose high-frequency sensitivity with age. It is a vital triple-award topic bridging wave mechanics with biological sensory systems.

core.h: Nature of Sound Waves in Solids
core.p: Sound waves are longitudinal waves that require a medium to travel. In solids, sound is transmitted through the parallel oscillation of particles, causing regions of compression and rarefaction.
bullets: Solids contain particles that are very close together and held tightly by strong chemical bonds.
When a solid is disturbed, particles collide rapidly with their neighbours, transferring kinetic energy efficiently.
Particles oscillate back and forth parallel to the direction of energy propagation.
Compressions are regions where particles are pushed closer together, resulting in higher local pressure.
Rarefactions are regions where particles are pulled further apart, resulting in lower local pressure.

callouts.p: A wave where the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to vibrate.

core.h: Why Sound Travels Faster in Solids than Gases
core.p: The speed of sound depends on the properties of the medium through which it travels, specifically its density and elastic stiffness. Solids have much higher elastic moduli than gases, enabling extremely rapid energy transfer.
bullets: Sound travels slowest in gases, faster in liquids, and fastest in solids.
The elastic properties of solids mean restoring forces between particles are exceptionally strong.
Particles return to their equilibrium positions much faster in solids than in gases or liquids.
Steel conducts sound at approximately 5900 m/s, compared to air at roughly 343 m/s at room temperature.
Temperature also affects speed: sound travels faster in warmer air because molecules have more kinetic energy.

callouts.p: Students often think sound is faster in solids just because they are denser. It is the high elasticity (stiffness) that primarily causes the high speed, outweighing the effect of high density.

core.h: How Sound Enters the Human Ear
core.p: Hearing is the biological process of converting airborne sound waves into electrochemical signals that the brain interprets as sound. This involves a sequence of mechanical transfers through the outer, middle, and inner ear.
bullets: The **pinna** (outer ear) funnels sound waves into the ear canal.
Sound waves travel down the ear canal and strike the **ear drum** (tympanic membrane).
Variations in air pressure cause the flexible ear drum to vibrate back and forth.
The frequency of the ear drum's vibration matches the frequency of the incoming sound wave.
The amplitude of the vibration corresponds to the volume or intensity of the sound.

callouts.p: The ear acts as a transducer, converting acoustic energy into mechanical energy, then hydraulic energy, and finally electrical nerve impulses.

core.h: The Ossicles and Middle Ear Amplification
core.p: The middle ear contains three tiny bones called ossicles, which bridge the air-filled outer ear to the fluid-filled inner ear.
bullets: The three bones are the **malleus** (hammer), **incus** (anvil), and **stapes** (stirrup).
The malleus is attached to the ear drum and passes vibrations to the incus, which passes them to the stapes.
The ossicles act as a mechanical lever system, amplifying the force of the vibrations.
The surface area of the ear drum is much larger than the oval window of the inner ear, further increasing pressure.
This amplification is essential because sound waves lose energy when passing from air into the denser fluid of the cochlea.

callouts.p: Always use the term **ossicles** and name at least two of the bones (malleus, incus, stapes) when asked about middle ear function.

core.h: The Cochlea and Hair Cells in the Inner Ear
core.p: The inner ear houses the cochlea, a snail shell-shaped structure filled with fluid and lined with specialized sensory receptors known as hair cells.
bullets: The stapes pushes against the **oval window**, creating pressure waves in the cochlear fluid.
Fluid movement causes the flexible basilar membrane inside the cochlea to vibrate.
Different frequencies of sound cause maximum vibration at different locations along the basilar membrane.
High-frequency sounds stimulate hair cells near the base of the cochlea; low-frequency sounds stimulate hair cells near the apex.
When hair cells are bent by fluid motion, they generate electrical signals.

callouts.p: A coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear containing the organ of Corti and auditory hair cells.

core.h: The Auditory Nerve and the Brain
core.p: Once mechanical vibrations are converted into electrical impulses by the hair cells, the auditory nerve transmits these signals to the brain for processing.
bullets: Electrical impulses travel along the **auditory nerve** directly to the auditory cortex in the brain.
The brain interprets the frequency of the impulses as pitch.
The brain interprets the rate of firing and number of activated hair cells as volume (loudness).
Without the brain's interpretation, hearing sound is impossible; the ear only detects physical stimuli.
Damage to the auditory nerve or brain cortex results in sensorineural deafness.

callouts.p: Hair cells -> Auditory nerve -> Brain (Auditory Cortex).

core.p: A healthy human ear can only detect sound waves within a specific band of frequencies, known as the human hearing range.
bullets: The typical hearing range for a healthy young human is **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz** (20 kHz).
Sounds below 20 Hz are classified as **infrasound**.
Sounds above 20,000 Hz are classified as **ultrasound**.
Neither infrasound nor ultrasound can be detected by the human ear.
The upper limit of human hearing is not fixed throughout life.

callouts.p: Do not confuse Hz with kHz. 20 kHz equals 20,000 Hz. Always check units in calculation and data analysis questions.

core.p: As humans age, physiological changes in the inner ear lead to a progressive loss of hearing sensitivity, particularly at high frequencies.
bullets: The condition of losing high-frequency hearing with age is called **presbycusis**.
Hair cells near the base of the cochlea (which detect high frequencies) degenerate over time due to wear and tear.
Older adults often struggle to hear high-pitched sounds like birds singing or a telephone ringing.
Exposure to loud noises over a lifetime accelerates the damage to auditory hair cells.
Hair cells in humans do not regenerate naturally once destroyed.

callouts.p: The gradual loss of hearing in both ears that commonly occurs as people age, particularly affecting high frequencies.

core.p: The human ear has distinct physical limitations regarding frequency and intensity, restricting the sounds we can perceive.
bullets: We cannot hear sounds below 20 Hz because the ear drum and ossicles cannot resonate effectively at such low frequencies.
We cannot hear sounds above 20,000 Hz because the basilar membrane and hair cells cannot respond quickly enough.
The threshold of hearing varies with frequency; humans are most sensitive to frequencies between 1,000 Hz and 4,000 Hz (human speech range).
Prolonged exposure to sounds above 85 dB can cause permanent hearing damage.
Some animals (e.g., dogs, bats, elephants) have evolved hearing ranges far outside human limits for survival.

callouts.p: Link animal hearing ranges (like dogs hearing up to 45,000 Hz) to the concept of ultrasound and adaptation.

core.p: Sound waves outside the human hearing range have important industrial, medical, and scientific applications.
bullets: **Infrasound** (<20 Hz): Used by scientists to monitor volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and meteor impacts.
**Ultrasound** (>20 kHz): Used in medicine for prenatal scanning without ionizing radiation.
Ultrasound is used industrially for non-destructive testing (NDT) to detect internal flaws in metal structures or pipes.
SONAR uses high-frequency sound waves to map the ocean floor and measure water depth.
Ultrasound reflects partially at boundaries between different media due to differences in acoustic impedance.

head: Type
Frequency
Key Application
rows: Detecting seismic activity and volcanic tremors
Medical scans, SONAR, and flaw detection

callouts.p: Unlike X-rays, ultrasound uses non-ionizing sound waves, making it safe for imaging developing fetuses.

analogy.t: The Domino Chain and the Factory Conveyor Belt
analogy.p: Imagine a long line of dominoes set up close together (representing solid particles). When you push the first one, it falls into the next instantly because they are tightly packed. This is like sound travelling fast through a solid. Now imagine the dominoes are spaced far apart across a large room (gas particles); it takes much longer for the energy to travel down the line. Where the analogy breaks down is that dominoes only fall once, whereas sound wave particles oscillate back and forth repeatedly around a fixed equilibrium position without permanently moving along with the wave.

terms.d: A wave where the particle oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are closest together.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are furthest apart.
The visible outer part of the ear that collects and funnels sound waves.
A thin, flexible membrane that vibrates when sound waves strike it.
Three tiny bones (malleus, incus, stapes) in the middle ear that amplify vibrations.
A coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear containing hair cells that detect sound.
The nerve that transmits electrical impulses from the cochlea to the brain.
Sound waves with frequencies below the lower limit of human hearing (under 20 Hz).
Sound waves with frequencies above the upper limit of human hearing (above 20,000 Hz).
Age-related hearing loss characterized by a reduced ability to hear high-frequency sounds.
A stiff structural element within the cochlea that separates two liquid-filled tubes and holds hair cells.

mistakes.w: Sound travels fastest in gases because they have more space.
mistakes.r: Sound travels fastest in solids because strong elastic bonds allow rapid particle interaction.

mistakes.w: The ear converts sound directly into electrical signals in the air.
mistakes.r: Sound is mechanical in the air/eardrum/ossicles, hydraulic in the cochlea, and electrical only at the hair cells and auditory nerve.

mistakes.w: Humans can hear all frequencies of sound.
mistakes.r: Human hearing is strictly limited to the range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

mistakes.w: Ultrasound is a type of X-ray used for scanning babies.
mistakes.r: Ultrasound is high-frequency sound waves, not electromagnetic radiation.

mistakes.w: Infrasound is sound that is too quiet to hear.
mistakes.r: Infrasound is sound with a frequency too low to hear (<20 Hz), regardless of its volume.

mistakes.w: Presbycusis is caused by listening to music too loudly once.
mistakes.r: Presbycusis is age-related hearing loss caused by gradual degeneration of hair cells over time.

mistakes.w: Sound waves carry matter along with them as they travel through a solid.
mistakes.r: Waves transfer energy, not matter; particles only oscillate about a fixed position.

exam.q: State the typical range of human hearing in Hertz.
model: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (allow 20 Hz to 20 kHz)
exam.tip: Memorize this range precisely. Do not mix up Hz and kHz.

exam.q: Explain why sound travels faster in steel than in air.
model: Steel has particles that are much closer together and held by stronger bonds / higher elasticity (1)
This allows restoring forces between particles to act much more rapidly (1)
Therefore, kinetic energy is transferred between particles faster in solids than in gases (1)
exam.tip: Mention elasticity and particle spacing, not just density.

exam.q: Describe the function of the ossicles in the human ear.
model: They amplify the vibrations / force of the sound waves (1)
They pass the vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window / inner ear (1)
exam.tip: Use the words amplify and pass vibrations for full marks.

exam.q: A student claims that a sound wave of frequency 15 Hz can be heard by humans. Explain why this claim is incorrect.
model: 15 Hz is below 20 Hz (1)
This is classified as infrasound which is outside the human hearing range (1)
exam.tip: State the lower limit of human hearing and name the frequency category (infrasound).

exam.q: Explain how the cochlea converts fluid pressure waves into electrical signals.
model: Pressure waves move the fluid inside the cochlea (1)

worked.q: A sound wave travels through a steel rail at 5900 m/s with a frequency of 295 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
steps: State the wave speed equation: v = f x lambda
Rearrange the equation to solve for wavelength: lambda = v / f
Substitute the values: lambda = 5900 / 295
Calculate the final answer: lambda = 20 metres

worked.q: An ultrasound scanner emits waves into human tissue where the wave speed is 1540 m/s. If an echo returns from a boundary in 0.00004 seconds (40 microseconds), calculate the depth of the boundary.
steps: Understand that the wave travels to the boundary and back, so total distance = v x t
Calculate total distance: distance = 1540 x 0.00004 = 0.0616 metres
Divide by 2 because the wave made a round trip (to and back): depth = 0.0616 / 2
Calculate final depth: depth = 0.0308 metres (or 30.8 mm)

phy_ocra.11.4.summary: When a wave meets the boundary (interface) between two materials, its energy can be **reflected** back, **transmitted** into the new material or **absorbed** by it, and usually all three happen at once in different proportions. Which outcome dominates depends on the **material**, the **surface** and the **wavelength** of the wave. Grade 9 answers link each outcome to what happens to the wave's energy and use correct ray-diagram language: normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, specular and diffuse reflection.

core.p: An **interface** is the boundary where one material meets another, for example air and glass, air and water, or air and a wall. When a wave arrives at an interface, the energy it carries has three possible fates. Usually the energy is **shared** between all three, so a pane of glass reflects a little light, absorbs a little and transmits most of it.
bullets: **Reflection**: the wave bounces back into the first material.
**Transmission**: the wave passes through into the second material (it may change direction, which is refraction).
**Absorption**: the wave's energy is taken in by the material, usually heating it up.
The proportions depend on the type of material, the surface texture and the wavelength (frequency) of the wave.
Energy is conserved: incident energy = reflected + transmitted + absorbed.

head: Outcome
Where the energy goes
Everyday example
rows: Image in a mirror, echo from a cliff
Black car roof warming in sunshine

callouts.p: Real interfaces almost never do only one thing. Say 'mostly reflected' or 'most energy is absorbed', not 'only'.

core.h: Reflection and the law of reflection
core.p: When a wave reflects from a flat surface it obeys the **law of reflection**: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the **normal**, an imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees to the surface at the point where the ray hits it. Measuring from the normal works for any surface shape, which is why physicists use it instead of the surface itself.
bullets: **Angle of incidence (i)**: angle between the incident ray and the normal.
**Angle of reflection (r)**: angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
Law of reflection: **i = r**.
The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
A ray hitting along the normal (i = 0) reflects straight back along itself.
Reflection does not change the wave's speed, frequency or wavelength, because it stays in the same medium.

callouts.p: A line drawn at right angles (90 degrees) to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
Measuring the angle from the mirror surface gives 90 minus the correct angle and loses the mark.

core.p: Whether you see an image depends on how smooth the surface is compared with the wavelength. A **smooth** surface such as a mirror or still water gives **specular reflection**: parallel rays stay parallel after reflecting, so a clear image forms. A **rough** surface such as paper gives **diffuse reflection**: the normal points in a different direction at every tiny bump, so each ray obeys i = r but the reflected rays scatter in many directions and no clear image forms.
bullets: Specular reflection: smooth surface, reflected rays parallel, clear image (mirror, calm lake).
Diffuse reflection: rough surface, reflected rays scattered, no image (paper, wall, clothing).
The law of reflection is still obeyed at every point in diffuse reflection; only the normals differ.
Diffuse reflection is why you can see a non-glowing object from any angle in a room.
What counts as rough depends on wavelength: a surface rough for light can be smooth for long radio waves.

callouts.p: Top answers say the surface is uneven so the normal is in a different direction at each point, so rays reflect at different angles.
